reference.source: Smith & Tanagho's General Urology / Campbell-Walsh Urology
clinicalPearls: Presents as the sudden, painful inability to pass urine with a palpable, tender, distended bladder that is dull to percussion
In men the commonest precipitant is benign prostatic obstruction, often triggered by infection, constipation, alcohol, immobility, or anticholinergic and sympathomimetic drugs
Immediate management is urgent bladder decompression with a urethral catheter; suprapubic catheterisation is used when urethral access fails or is contraindicated
Painless retention with a grossly distended bladder suggests chronic-on-acute (high-pressure or high-residual) retention rather than a purely acute event
Record the drained volume; a large residual and any renal impairment point toward chronic high-pressure retention with risk of post-obstructive diuresis
Post-obstructive diuresis after decompression can cause marked fluid and electrolyte losses, requiring monitoring of urine output, weight, and electrolytes
A trial without catheter, often facilitated by an alpha-blocker, is appropriate once the precipitant is treated; failure indicates need for ongoing catheterisation or definitive surgery
Always exclude and treat urinary infection, and consider spinal cord compression or cauda equina when neurological features accompany retention
reference.pathophysiology: Acute urinary retention is the abrupt failure to empty the bladder, arising from mechanical obstruction (most often prostatic enlargement, but also urethral stricture, clot, or stone), increased outlet tone, impaired detrusor contractility, or neurogenic causes. Bladder overdistension raises intravesical pressure and, in high-pressure chronic retention, is transmitted to the upper tracts causing hydronephrosis and renal impairment. Precipitating factors such as anticholinergic drugs, alpha-agonists, infection, pain, and prostatic congestion tip a compensated bladder into decompensation and acute failure to void.
additionalDifferentials: Constipation or pelvic mass causing extrinsic compression
additionalInvestigations: Bladder ultrasound to confirm distension and measure retained volume
Urinalysis and culture to identify infection
Serum creatinine and electrolytes to detect obstructive renal impairment
Renal tract ultrasound to assess for hydronephrosis in suspected chronic retention
PSA (interpreted with caution, as retention and catheterisation raise levels)
Neurological assessment and spinal imaging when cauda equina or cord compression is suspected
redFlags: Acute urinary retention is itself a urological emergency requiring immediate bladder decompression
High-pressure chronic retention with hydronephrosis and renal impairment
Post-obstructive diuresis causing dehydration and electrolyte disturbance after decompression
Retention with saddle anaesthesia, bilateral leg symptoms, or bowel dysfunction suggesting cauda equina syndrome
Associated fever or urosepsis in an obstructed system
reference.prognosis: Prompt decompression relieves symptoms rapidly; many men can eventually void after a trial without catheter and treatment of precipitants, but recurrent retention often signals the need for definitive prostatic surgery, and delayed relief risks lasting renal damage.
pitfalls: Delaying catheterisation and allowing prolonged painful overdistension
Missing high-pressure chronic retention by not measuring residual volume or checking renal function
Failing to anticipate and monitor for post-obstructive diuresis
Overlooking neurological causes such as cauda equina compression
Rapid complete decompression without awareness of possible haematuria ex vacuo
management: Relieve retention immediately by draining the bladder with a urethral catheter, using suprapubic catheterisation when urethral access fails or is contraindicated
Identify and reverse precipitants: stop anticholinergic and sympathomimetic drugs, relieve constipation, and treat infection and pain
Start an alpha-blocker such as tamsulosin before a trial without catheter in men with benign prostatic obstruction, adding a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor for a large prostate
Anticipate and manage post-obstructive diuresis with monitoring of urine output, weight and electrolytes and appropriate fluid replacement
Record the drained volume and check renal function and the upper tracts to identify high-pressure chronic retention
Arrange a trial without catheter and refer for definitive prostatic surgery such as transurethral resection when this fails or retention recurs
Escalate to urgent neurosurgical or spinal assessment when cauda equina or cord compression is suspected
